source.title: Report from the Open Problems Session at OPSFA13

accepted.question_text: For the quartic polynomial x^2(x-y)(x-z) + y^2(y-x)(y-z) + z^2(z-x)(z-y), which is nonnegative for all real x, y, z and falls into Hilbert's exceptional three-variable degree-four sum-of-squares case, find an explicit representation of this polynomial as a sum of squares of real polynomials.

evidence.quote: There is a strange theorem of Hilbert [23]. He proved that if one has a polynomial in k variables which is homogeneous of degree j and which is nonnegative for all real values of the variables, then it can be written as a sum of k squares when either k or j is 2, and when k = 3 and j = 4, but not necessarily in all other cases. The case n = 2 ﬁts the exceptional condition k = 3, j = 4, so a natural question is: what is this representation? This problem has been solved in the mean time.

accepted.question_text: Let {P_n(x)} be an orthogonal polynomial sequence defined by P_n(x) = (x-c_n)P_{n-1}(x) - λ_n P_{n-2}(x) for n ≥ 1, with P_{-1}(x)=0, P_0(x)=1, each c_n real, each λ_n > 0, c_n → ∞, and λ_{n+1}/(c_n c_{n+1}) → 1/4. If x_{n,1} < \cdots < x_{n,n} are the zeros of P_n, ξ_i = lim_{n→∞} x_{n,i}, η_j = lim_{n→∞} x_{n,n-j+1}, σ = lim_{i→∞} ξ_i, and τ = lim_{j→∞} η_j, then in the difficult one-quarter-class case σ = -∞ and τ = ∞, is there an analogue of Blumenthal's theorem describing the limiting distribution of the zeros for this unbounded situation?
accepted.context_brief: One-quarter class analogue of Blumenthal theorem

evidence.quote: We would like to ﬁnd analogues of these theorems when the sequences above are unbounded. To this end, let us consider the “one quarter class” of orthogonal polynomials (see [10]); namely, let lim n→∞ cn = ∞, and lim n→∞ λn+1/(cncn+1) = 1/4. ... This now leaves the most diﬃcult case, σ = −∞. We thus pose the inevitable question: Is there an analog of Blumenthal’s theorem for this case?

accepted.question_text: Within the same one-quarter-class setting for orthogonal polynomial sequences, are there examples other than the Meixner polynomials of the second kind (the Meixner-Pollaczek polynomials) whose orthogonality measure has spectrum extending over the entire real line, corresponding to the case σ = -∞?

evidence.quote: The lack of speciﬁc examples of OPS whose orthogonality measure has a spectrum extending over the entire real line makes this situation the most diﬃcult to conjecture about. The only known example of OPS of this type, are the Meixner polynomials of the second kind [8] (i.e., the so-called “Meixner–Pollaczek” polynomials). Do there exist any other OPS examples of this type?

accepted.question_text: Given a hypergeometric orthogonal polynomial family P_n(x; a) with parameters a and a connection relation expressing P_n(x; a) in another parameter family P_k(x; b), obtain closed-form expressions for the generalized linearization coefficients γ_{k,m,n}(a,b) in expansions of the form P_m(x; a)P_n(x; a) = Σ_{k=0}^{m+n} γ_{k,m,n}(a,b) P_k(x; b), ideally in hypergeometric closed form for families such as Gegenbauer and continuous q-ultraspherical/Rogers polynomials and, if possible, more broadly in the (q-)Askey scheme.

evidence.quote: Given a hypergeometric orthogonal polynomial Pn(x; a), where a is a set of arbitrary parameters, we would like to obtain closed-form expressions for the coeﬃcients of generalized linearization formulas.

The best chance for ﬁnding generalized linearization coeﬃcients which are hypergeometric functions is for the Gegenbauer and continuous q-ultraspherical/Rogers polynomials. This is because these linearization coeﬃcients are given by products of Pochhammer symbols. Perhaps other orthogonal polynomials in the (q-)Askey scheme are amenable to this calculation, but we have yet to uncover further closed-form linearization formulae.

accepted.question_text: Develop a systematic method for simplifying multiple hypergeometric summations and iterated-integral-derived sums to lower-order sums, ideally to single-sum or other recognizably closed forms when such reductions exist, using a combination of algorithmic tools such as holonomic-systems or difference-field methods together with whatever structural insight is needed to identify the correct reduced form.

evidence.quote: Here we describe a general problem area, rather than a speciﬁc open problem. In various computations, such as connection coeﬃcients of families of orthogonal polynomials, or multiple iterated integrals, one arrives at a multiple sum of hypergeometric form. ... What is needed is a systematic approach to ﬁnd simpliﬁcation to lower order summations when this is possible, or hopefully, when the answer is known.

accepted.question_text: Does there exist an algorithm that efficiently converts between values of a function sampled on a grid on the sphere and its spherical harmonic coefficients in both directions, with ideal complexity on the order of O(n log n) for a grid of n points?

evidence.quote: Does there exist an algorithm that can eﬃciently convert from values of a function evaluated on a grid on the sphere to spherical harmonic coeﬃcients, and vice-versa? Ideally, such an algorithm would be roughly of complexity O(n log n) for a grid of n points.

accepted.question_text: Can one create easy-to-use software that, for a general family of orthogonal polynomials specified for example by a weight function, returns uniform asymptotic expansions together with error bounds, so that non-experts can reliably use these asymptotics in applications such as quadrature and fast transforms?

evidence.quote: Is it possible to make uniform asymptotics with error bounds easy-to-use, for general orthogonal polynomials? ... A software package that would take in a general weight and return the uniform asymptotic expansion would be ideal.

accepted.question_text: What is the finite-dimensional spectrum of a random symmetric Bernoulli matrix, that is, a symmetric matrix whose entries are independently chosen as ±1 subject to symmetry, beyond the asymptotic universality statements known for Wigner ensembles?

evidence.quote: What is the spectrum of a ﬁnite-dimensional random symmetric Bernoulli matrix? A random symmetric Bernoulli matrix consists of entries that are randomly ±1, subject to a symmetry condition. What is the spectrum of a ﬁnite-dimensional random symmetric Bernoulli matrix? Unlike other symmetric random matrices such as Gaussian Orthogonal Ensemble (GOE), these only have a ﬁnite number of conﬁgurations of eigenvalues. While such matrices fall into the general framework of universality for Wigner ensembles [19, 38] (describing the asymptotics of the spectrum), this does not explain the ﬁnite-dimensional picture.

accepted.question_text: Does there exist, for general invariant random-matrix ensembles, a corresponding Wigner-like family having the same limiting spectral density, analogous to the way Wigner ensembles correspond to Gaussian Unitary Ensembles and Wishart ensembles correspond to Laguerre Unitary Ensembles?

evidence.quote: Does there exist a Wigner-like family corresponding to general invariant ensembles? For special cases we know such families exist. For example, the Wigner ensembles have the same limiting spectral density as a Gaussian Unitary Ensemble (GUE). Similarly, the Wishart ensembles have the same limiting spectral density as a Laguerre Unitary Ensembles (LUE).

accepted.question_text: Let δ > 0, λ > 0, n ∈ N_0, and for 0 < t < π define F_n^{λ,δ}(t) = ∫_0^t (t-θ)^δ C_n^λ(cos θ) (sin θ)^{2λ} dθ, where C_n^λ is the Gegenbauer polynomial. Is it true that F_n^{λ,δ}(t) > 0 for all t in (0, π] if and only if δ ≥ λ + 1?

evidence.quote: Conjecture 6.1. Let δ > 0, λ > 0 and n ∈ N0. For every 0 < t < π, deﬁne F λ,δ n (t) = ∫ t 0 (t−θ)δ C λ n (cos θ)(sin θ)2λ dθ. Then F λ,δ n (t) > 0 for all t in (0, π] if and only if δ ≥ λ + 1.

accepted.question_text: Define polynomials Ã_n(t) by the recurrence (n^3 - (-1)^n t^3)Ã_{n-1}(t) + (2n+1)nÃ_n(t) - (n+1)^2 nÃ_{n+1}(t) = 0 and suppose they are the partial sums Ã_n(t) = Σ_{k=0}^n A_k(t) arising from the related recurrence for A_n(t). Can one deduce directly from this recurrence that lim_{n→∞} Ã_n(t) = ∏_{j=1}^∞ (1 + t^3/(8j^3))?

evidence.quote: Equivalently, the polynomials ˜An(t) = n∑ k=0 Ak(t) that come from the recursion (n3− (−1)nt3)˜An−1 + (2n + 1)n˜An− (n + 1)2n˜An+1 = 0 (7.1) satisfy lim n→∞ ˜An(t) = ∞∏ j=1 (1 + t3/(8j3)).
Questions 7.1. Is there an argument to deduce the limit of ˜An(t) as n → ∞ using the recurrence relation for the polynomials (7.1)?

accepted.question_text: Let A_n(t) be the polynomials determined by (n^3 - (-1)^n t^3)A_n(t) + (n+1)^2(2n+1)A_{n+1}(t) + (n+2)^2(n+1)A_{n+2}(t) = 0 with A_0=1 and A_1=0, and let Ã_n(t) = Σ_{k=0}^n A_k(t). Can the polynomial families A_n(t) and Ã_n(t) be expressed explicitly in hypergeometric form?
accepted.context_brief: Hypergeometric forms for A_n and partial sums

evidence.quote: the polynomials An(t) ∈ Q[t3] (of degree [n/2] in x = t3) produced by the recursion (n3− (−1)nt3)An(t) + (n + 1)2(2n + 1)An+1(t) + (n + 2)2(n + 1)An+2(t) = 0 and the initial conditions A0 = 1, A1 = 0 (no closed-form is known!)
Questions 7.1. ... Can the polynomials An(t) and ˜An(t) be given in an explicit hypergeometric form?
